abstract: The mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is a multi-copy genome present in most eukaryotic cells and essential for life. The presence of different mtDNA variants within a cell, or heteroplasmy, may cause pathology when the level of deleterious variants exceeds a critical threshold. However, the mechanisms that control heteroplasmy levels remain poorly understood, in part due to a lack of technologies to visualise mtDNA heteroplasmy in situ and correlate it with intracellular processes. mtDNA single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridisation (mtDNA-smFISH) allows in situ visualisation of mtDNA molecules and sequence-specific detection of heteroplasmic variants. Here, we provide protocols for sequence-specific detection of mtDNA, large-scale single mtDNA deletions and species-specific haplotypes, in fixed human and Drosophila cells and in whole-mount Drosophila tissues. Combining mtDNA-smFISH with immunohistochemistry using biotin-labelled primary antibodies that resist heat-based denaturation, allows concomitant detection of intracellular proteins. We further describe two image-analysis pipelines, one for 3D quantification and one open-source for 2D quantification of mtDNA deletions in Drosophila tissues and cell culture. This enables estimation of single-cell heteroplasmy levels, observation of cell-to-cell variability, and detection of mtDNA variants at a subcellular level, making mtDNA-smFISH a powerful tool to study the intracellular processes regulating heteroplasmy and mtDNA quality control.
